item.title: Meta-learning attentional strategies in multidimensional reinforcement learning
item.description:
Relevance: 35% | Source: SocArXiv
Zhang Chen et al.
Reward learning in complex, multidimensional environments requires balancing abstract generalisation with stimulus-specific precision. Previous work suggests that humans initially rely on feature-based abstraction to support fast generalisation, before shifting toward more precise, object-based learning. We asked whether humans also generalise these attentional strategies to novel contexts. In a large-scale study (N = 350), participants learned reward contingencies in an environment where one feature dimension (colour or pattern) was informative at a group level but imperfectly predictive at the stimulus level. In a subsequent phase with novel stimuli, the informative dimension either remained stable (Repeat) or changed (Switch). Average accuracy performance was similar between conditions, yet computational modelling revealed a divergence in strategy: when the relevant dimension remained stable, participants maintained a hybrid approach; when it switched, participants showed a tendency toward object- based learning, reducing reliance on feature-based abstraction. Time-resolved analyses showed that this reconfiguration began almost immediately upon entering the new context. Humans therefore tune the level of abstraction they use based on inferred environmental reliability, striking a balance between rapid generalisation and stimulus-specific precision

item.title: Behaviorally driven increased glutamatergic activity from lateral entorhinal cortex to hippocampus supports object and spatial memory recall
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Hernandez-Frausto, M., Samchok, T., Johnson, C. D., Bilash, O. M., Tai, J., Basu, J.
Interactions between the entorhinal cortex (EC) and hippocampal area CA1 are vital for episodic memory formation, but their role in recall is less clear. Canonically, spatial processing -- the "where" of an experience -- is attributed to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), whereas the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) processes the "what": non-spatial sensory cues and objects. Though these inputs are anatomically segregated in CA1, multimodal memory processing requires integrating spatial and contextual information, and recent work suggests greater MEC-LEC crosstalk than previously thought. Global LEC silencing via lesions, or combined suppression of glutamatergic and GABAergic LEC neurons, impairs associational goal-oriented learning and multi-object-cued encoding. However, the role of LEC glutamatergic projections specifically to CA1 during recall in freely moving spatial behaviors, and their contribution to synaptic plasticity, remains unclear. We used fiber photometry to record LEC axonal calcium dynamics in CA1 during novel object recognition and Barnes maze tasks, and ex vivo electrophysiology with LEC optogenetic activation. LEC activity increased during recall in both tasks, especially as animals learned spatial cues, peaking at late training stages of the Barnes maze. Local chemogenetic silencing of LEC inputs in CA1 after learning impaired recall. Ex vivo, temporally precise optogenetic activation of LEC input paired with CA3 intrahippocampal inputs was sufficient to induce long-term potentiation of both pathways in CA1 pyramidal neurons. These results suggest that LEC glutamatergic input to CA1 is dynamically modulated by experience to support recall during both object recognition and spatial navigation, with a functional role in synaptic plasticity.

item.title: Olfactory-Visual Integration Facilitates Scene Perception through Modulation of the Parahippocampal Place Area
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Wang, Y., Chen, K., Wu, Y., Zhou, W.
Visual scenes anchor our experience of the world, yet the places in which scenes unfold are defined not only by what we see but also by what we smell. Whether and how odors contribute to the neural representation of visual scenes remains poorly understood. Here we asked whether a semantically congruent odor facilitates scene perception and identified the neural mechanisms supporting this facilitation. In two behavioral experiments, participants judged whether briefly presented, masked images depicted intact or scrambled scenes while continuously smelling an odor. A congruent odor lowered the exposure duration needed for accurate scene detection, and a placebo experiment, in which participants merely believed they were smelling an odor, failed to reproduce this benefit, indicating that the facilitation depends on actual sensory input rather than semantic priming. In an fMRI experiment, congruent odors enhanced responses and sharpened category-level scene representations in the parahippocampal place area (PPA), with the congruency-driven enhancement localized to the same anterior subregion that encoded scene identity. A conjunction analysis revealed superadditive responses to congruent odor-scene pairs in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and hippocampus, and psychophysiological interaction analyses showed that congruent stimulation strengthened functional coupling among the OFC, PPA, and piriform cortex. Notably, the piriform cortex decoded visual scene identity after congruent odor-scene pairing, suggesting that odor-scene binding extends scene representations into primary olfactory cortex. Together, these findings identify the PPA as a site where olfactory signals refine the neural code for visual scenes and reveal an OFC-coordinated piriform-OFC-PPA network through which smell shapes our sense of place.

item.title: Is short-term storage correlated with fluid intelligence? Strategy use explains the apparent relationship between ‘number of remembered items’ and fluid intelligence
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: SocArXiv
Mark Schurgin et al.
Working memory is a core cognitive system that actively maintains information in an accessible state to support a variety of everyday tasks. Working memory performance has frequently been shown to strongly correlate with fluid intelligence, particularly when tasks involve a high degree of manipulation and executive function, as opposed to solely utilizing short-term storage capacity. However, recent work has claimed that simple storage capacity is also correlated with fluid intelligence, and that this is driven by a particularly special and dissociable component of capacity, the ‘number of items represented’ (rather than the precision of those representations). Here we demonstrate that such correlations do not arise solely or primarily from simple storage capacity (nor a single dissociable component of capacity), but are driven by the availability and usage of different kinds of visual representations to represent the stimuli. We found that despite being probed on the same items, with the same foils, at the same set size, only working memory displays that allowed for the use of both item and ensemble representations correlated with fluid intelligence. These results provide evidence against the hypothesis that simple storage alone is related to fluid intelligence. They also demonstrate that participants make use of more complex and structured representations rather than solely individual item representation, even in simple storage tasks, and suggest that strategic utilization of these representations may be, in such situations, what drives correlations with fluid intelligence.

item.title: Inferred interactions transform values into lattice-patterned choice attractors in orbitofrontal cortex
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Zhang, K., Kanazawa, Y., Crimmins, T. G., Padoa-Schioppa, C., Tavoni, G.
Economic decisions require transforming option values into choices, a process involving the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), but the circuit mechanism remains unclear. We recorded OFC activity in monkeys performing a juice-choice task, fitted graphical Ising models to spike data, and simulated the inferred networks. Offer inputs shifted the networks toward attractor states favoring the choice representation supported by relative value. Targeted ablations revealed a core functional backbone for this transformation, linking offer-value and choice-tuned populations, alongside amplification by broader network interactions and complementary contributions from positive- and negative-encoding pathways. Mean interactions between tuning groups captured the average transformation, while finer interaction structure shaped its network-specific implementation. At single-neuron resolution, the transformation was expressed through a recurring response motif coupling activation and suppression in a spatial lattice. Together, these results reveal how inferred OFC interactions transform offer values into choice-selective attractor states and shape the lattice-patterned neuronal recruitment characterizing this transformation.

item.title: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv AI
Yechan Cho, Hyeonsu Lee, Emma Deneuville, Jaeson Jang
arXiv:2611.33615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that remains challenging for modern vision-language models. Meanwhile, number sense is already present in numerically na\"ive animals, suggesting that it can emerge without explicit numerical learning. Deep neural networks provide a related observation, with numerosity-selective units appearing after training on unrelated natural-image tasks and even before any training. However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.

item.title: Resource-State Modulation of Prefrontal Value Processing during Earning-Spending Decision Making
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Wang, H., Si, H., Zhu, L., Yang, T.
Money mediates earning and spending, and accumulated monetary holdings constitute both a basic form of wealth and an external resource state that shapes economic decisions. Unlike internal physiological states such as hunger or satiety, external resources persist outside the body, can be acquired or depleted through choice, and preserve access to future consumption. Although money and wealth are human constructs, balancing resource acquisition and consumption may rely on evolutionarily conserved neural computations. Here we investigated these computations using an earning-spending task, in which rhesus monkeys chose between earning virtual tokens and spending accumulated tokens for water, with holdings carrying across trials. As holdings varied, monkeys shifted between earning and spending choices. A state-dependent utility model explained this shift through opposing changes in the relative values of earning and spending. We recorded single-unit activities from the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Neuronal populations across all three regions represented current holdings, while ACC and OFC updated these representations after earning and spending outcomes. Crucially, resource state modulated value coding and reshaped the geometry of earning- and spending-value representations across all three regions. OFC exhibited a broader spectrum of signals spanning option value, chosen value, and good-based choice, whereas DLPFC representations were weighted more strongly toward action-based choice. Together, these findings identify distributed prefrontal mechanisms that represent, update, and use an external resource state to guide valuation and choice, extending neural accounts of state-dependent valuation beyond internal physiological conditions and suggesting an evolutionarily conserved foundation for balancing resource acquisition and consumption.

item.title: Top-down prefrontal connectivity accompanies perceptual breakthrough after interocular suppression
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Bandara, K. H., Rowe, E. G., Carter, O., Garrido, M. I.
The role of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in the emergence of visual stimuli into conscious awareness remains contested. Additionally, whether top-down prefrontal connectivity is shaped by prior expectations during this process is not well understood. To address these questions, we applied dynamic causal modelling (DCM) to an EEG dataset during breaking continuous flash suppression (bCFS), which offers tight control over when a stimulus breaks into conscious perception. Our network comprised bilateral PFC, primary visual cortex, fusiform gyrus and motor cortex. Because perceptual breakthrough precedes behavioural report, we used a temporally resolved classifier to empirically define each participants moment of perceptual breakthrough (M = 1250ms, SD = 100ms). DCMs were then inverted over this time window up until each individuals breakthrough point. Parametric empirical Bayes revealed that top-down connectivity from the PFC to all regions was necessary to explain the observed neural dynamics (posterior probability [pp] > 0.99), though evidence that this top-down influence was modulated by expectation was inconclusive (pp = 0.74). Together, these findings suggest that top-down PFC connectivity accompanies perceptual breakthrough in bCFS, but it remains unclear whether this is modulated by expectation.

item.title: Biphasic ERP Responses to Contextual Incongruency Across Algebraic, Graphical, and Lexical Domains
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: SocArXiv
María Guadalupe Yáñez-Ramos
Behavioral and EEG data from a contextual congruency task involving algebraic, graphical, and lexical sequences. The repository includes original recordings, participant-level ERPs, individualized measures of biphasic ERP dynamics, participant metadata, and experimental materials. The primary analytic sample comprises 42 participants. Analysis code: https://github.com/LupitaYanez/crossDomain-biphasicERPs

item.title: Features of Perceptual Grouping
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: SocArXiv
Gregory Francis
Visual elements often seem to group together in a way that dramatically affects the interpretation of a visual scene. Despite playing an important role in many aspects of visual perception, the mechanisms for forming groups and the representation of group-level information remains poorly understood. The LAMINART model of visual perception has successfully explained some aspects of texture perception and various visual tasks that implicitly involve grouping so we applied it to a direct measure of grouping. The model proposes that grouping is reflected, in part, by amodal connections being formed between disparate visual elements. The connection creation process is influenced by top-down control, which enables an observer to apply a connection strategy that changes the representation of visual information and thereby alters the perceived group. We apply the model to stimuli used in a replication study of Quinlan and Wilton (1998), which had observers rate how strongly a central target shape grouped with flankers to the left or right. The replication study largely validated the original study and noted that different observers seemed to use different approaches to creating groups. We show that the model can accommodate these differences and that combining the various models leads to a good explanation of the rating data. This project contains a version of the experiment that will run in a web browser, all gathered data, R scripts for the reported data analyses, and Python code for all model simulations.

item.title: Dissociation of Reward Incentive and Motivational Drive by Distinct Neural Circuits in Mice
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Takemoto, M., Song, W.-J.
The generation of reward incentive value and maintenance of motivational drive are distinct processes in reward-related behavior. However, how neural circuits differentially process these components remains poorly understood. Although intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS) paradigms have been utilized to identify reward-related circuits, ICSS measures may conflate reinitiated actions attributed to learned incentive value with ongoing motivated behavior sustained by concurrent stimulation. Here, we reveal a dissociation between these processes by optogenetically stimulating fibers in the stria terminalis bundle projecting to the medial nucleus accumbens (STBmNAc) and those in the medial forebrain bundle originating from the lateral NAc (MFBlNAc). We found that STBmNAc stimulation facilitated the reinitiation of ICSS actions, whereas MFBlNAc stimulation sustained ongoing ICSS behavior. Moreover, shortening the stimulation duration in STBmNAc mice increased the likelihood of subsequent re-engagement of stimulation-seeking. Additionally, STBmNAc stimulation, but not MFBlNAc stimulation, could substitute for primary rewards and support the acquisition of sensory cue-dependent operant behavior. Together, our findings suggest that STBmNAc activation promotes reward-anticipatory behavior by conferring reward incentive value, whereas MFBlNAc activation sustains ongoing behavior by maintaining motivational drive. Thus, reward-related behavior may not be governed by a unitary motivational system but may involve anatomically and functionally distinct neural components.

item.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Bianca Raimondi, Maurizio Gabbrielli
arXiv:2602.17229v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of the levels of complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different Bloom levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve high accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing evidence that level information is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model organizes representations according to Bloom categories early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

item.title: A Geometric View for Understanding Concept Learning and Neuron Interpretation in Sparse Autoencoders
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI
Chenhao Zhang, Chris Lin, Xiaojian Chen, Hanqi Feng, Su-In Lee
arXiv:2606.07007v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a unified mathematical framework for a geometric understanding of concept learning and neuron interpretation in sparse autoencoders (SAEs). While SAEs improve interpretability of neural networks by learning sparse feature representations, a principled definition of ''concept'' and ''learning'' remains unclear. We formalize concepts as sets of data points and cast concept learning as a set-alignment problem between human-defined and model-induced concepts. This formulation distinguishes three increasingly strong notions of learning -- detection, separation, and approximation -- and yields geometric conditions, error bounds, and capacity constraints for when concepts can be represented by individual neurons or multi-neuron units. It also provides a set-theoretic account for common SAE phenomena, including feature splitting, feature absorption, feature families, and hierarchical concepts. Finally, we connect concept learning and neuron interpretation through formal concept analysis, showing that the two directions need not agree and that their many-to-many structure can be organized by concept lattices. Experiments on synthetic data with ReLU and Top-$K$ SAEs illustrate the theory and reveal the effects of SAE size and sparsity on concept learning.

item.title: A Graph Signal Processing Perspective on Numerical Sequence Representations in LLM In-Context Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI
Jiajun Bao, Zihao Qi, Toni J. B. Liu, Gurbir Arora, Rapha\"el Sarfati, Nicolas Boull\'e, Christopher J. Earls
arXiv:2608.03015v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated in-context learning (ICL) capabilities for numerical inference over sequences serialized as text. Prior work has identified and characterized this form of numerical inference primarily through output-level evaluations such as prediction error. However, how numerical information is organized within LLM representations remains much less understood. To study this internal organization, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective in which attention induces a weighted graph over tokens, while token hidden states define signals on its nodes. Quantitative graph-spectral diagnostics and qualitative token-graph visualizations reveal that representations become more clearly differentiated by input dynamical complexity as context length increases. Simpler inputs produce attention-induced token graphs with stronger global connectivity and smoother, spectrally concentrated hidden-state signals, whereas more complex inputs produce more localized graphs and hidden-state signals with broader spectral support and greater high-frequency energy. These diagnostics and visualizations offer an interpretable view of the internal structure associated with numerical ICL, beyond what output-level prediction error alone reveals. Together, these findings point to systematic, context-dependent internal signatures associated with numerical ICL that are qualitatively conserved across model families.

item.title: Disciplined Anthropomorphism: How to Extend Cognitive Language to Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Matthieu Queloz
arXiv:2611.34090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers increasingly describe AI in cognitive terms such as "understanding" and "believing", while critics denounce this as wishful anthropomorphism. Both sides align in taking a subsumptive approach, however: they ask whether AI systems fall under concepts minted for human beings, reporting verdicts as discoveries about those systems when they are largely determined by conceptual frames. Yet the problem AI poses is precisely the problem of how to conceptually frame these systems, and the explosive rise of anthropomorphism is best seen as a response to this problem that needs disciplining rather than discouragement. A disciplined anthropomorphism, I argue, should disentangle the inferential connections bundled up in our cognitive concepts and ask which connections to preserve, sever, or forge for AI. The disciplining then comes, on the one hand, from the human conceptual needs that give point to the drawing of these connections and motivate the concepts' extension in the first place; and, on the other hand, from empirical and especially mechanistic evidence that supports and constrains these connections. By reverse-engineering a concept's point in relation to a particular need before re-engineering it to better serve that point in our dealings with AI, anthropomorphizing extensions can be point-based, transposing the work those concepts do for us while revising the inferential workings through which they do it. Transposing human-tailored conceptions of understanding and belief on the pivot of the underlying conceptual needs gives us just the definitional freedom required to accommodate how AI systems differ from us, yielding conceptions that are not just thinned-out versions of existing ones, but potentially richer and better fitted to the peculiarities of AI.

item.title: Encoding models uncover fine-grained feature selectivity for bodies, hands and tools
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: SocArXiv
Davide Cortinovis
Abstract: Occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) contains multiple regions that respond preferentially to the same category. Yet, regions selective for the same category may differ in their functional profile depending on their cortical location. Prior work suggests these functionally similar areas may serve different computational roles, motivating a systematic comparison of their broader response profiles beyond their shared category preference. Here, we collected densely sampled fMRI data from three participants scanned across six sessions, and combine image-level analyses with artificial neural network (ANN)-based encoding models to characterize the functional profiles of body-, hand-, and tool-selective areas in ventral and lateral OTC. Category-specific encoding models accurately predicted held-out images within the fMRI stimulus set, and generated predictions for millions of novel images. The highest-ranked images confirmed each region’s expected category preference. Critically, direct comparison between models of regions selective for the same category revealed systematic differences associated with their cortical location (lateral vs. ventral OTC) or hemispheric lateralization (left vs. right), consistent with previously reported functional distinctions. Specifically, the lateral OTC tool model was tuned to canonical tools and handheld manipulable objects, whereas its ventral counterpart showed broader tuning to inanimate objects. Similarly, the left lateral OTC hand model showed relatively stronger predicted responses to end-effector objects whereas the right lateral OTC hand model favoured whole-bodies. These findings show that areas sharing the same functional label (e.g., “hand selective”) can differ in their relative category preference, and that ANN-based encoding models can characterize those differences at a scale unobtainable with conventional designs.

item.title: Learning World Models through Contrastive Identification of Actions
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv AI
Hayeong Lee, Youngjun Suh, Byung-Jun Lee
arXiv:2611.32776v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.

item.title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Xueyang Yu, Yifan Jing, Taiming Lu, Linrong Cai, Zhipeng Cai, Yunyang Xiong, Gabriel Sarch, Zhuang Liu
arXiv:2611.34935v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.

item.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Ross Murphy, Gabriel Brostow
arXiv:2611.33304v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.

item.title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Yilin Luo, Jin Hwa Lee, Andrew M. Saxe, Antonio Sclocchi
arXiv:2611.33302v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.
